hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? has one person ever changed the direction of your life?
options: that’s how it often starts. listen.
maybe soon. this story is about that.

steps.line: In 1244, in the city of Konya, in today’s Turkey, Rumi was a respected Muslim scholar and teacher, with books, students and a fine name.
Then a wandering stranger came to town: Shams of Tabriz. In one popular telling, he found Rumi reading beside a pool.
steps.label: one popular telling

steps.q: Shams looks at Rumi’s precious books. What do you think he does?
steps.why: Into the pool. Shams had a way of shaking people awake.

steps.line: Shams tossed the books into the water. Rumi cried out. Shams lifted them out, dry. “What is this?” Rumi asked. “Something you don’t know yet.”
steps.label: one popular telling

steps.line: The two became inseparable. Rumi’s students grew jealous. Then one day Shams was gone, and no one knows for sure what happened.

steps.q: Shams left Konya once before, for Damascus. What did Rumi do?
o: Let him go, and went back to teaching
Sent his own son to bring him back
Closed his school and left Konya
steps.why: His son Sultan Walad found Shams in Damascus and brought him home. When Shams vanished the second time, Rumi went searching himself, and came back with poems.

steps.line: Out of the loss came an ocean of poems. His great work, the Masnavi, begins with a reed flute, crying.
The reed was cut from its reed bed. Every note it plays, Rumi says, is a song of longing to go back home.

steps.q: Why would a reed flute, the ney, be such a good picture of a longing soul?
o: It’s hollow, and sings only when breathed into
It was the easiest flute to make
It plays only in a minor key
steps.why: A ney must be cut, dried and hollowed before it can sing. Many Sufis read it as the self, emptied, so the breath of God can play through.

steps.line: Today his name is on poems shared on phones every day, often with his faith left out. He was a Muslim scholar, and his poems are full of the Qur’an.
steps.label: today

steps.q: After Rumi died, his followers founded the Mevlevi order. What are they famous for?
o: Chanting in the desert at night
Turning, slowly, in a whirling prayer
steps.why: The Mevlevi sema is a turning prayer to the ney: right palm up to receive, left palm down to pass it on. It’s remembrance of God, not a show.

say: here’s what i love. rumi was already wise and respected. then a friend turned his whole life over, and the grief became poetry.

in sufi teaching, the reed is the soul, cut from its source, which is god, and longing to return. love is the road back. and a famous saying credited to him, in a modern english version, imagines a field past all the arguing about right and wrong, where he’ll meet you.

steps.q: Rumi lost his closest friend, then wrote about a reed cut from its bed. What might the reed have meant, for him?
o: Only his grief for his lost friend
His childhood home, left behind for good
His grief for Shams, and for God
steps.why: Many readers hear both: missing a friend opened a deeper missing, the soul’s longing for God, its first home.

today.say: today, think of one person you’ve been at odds with, even a little. don’t fix anything. just picture a wide field, and the two of you walking into it from opposite sides. meet me there.
options: then let there be room for both of you.
good. no arguing in the field.

card.keepWhy: The reed sings because it remembers home.
sources: Rumi, Masnavi 1.1–18, the song of the reed (E. H. Whinfield, 1898: “Hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, Lamenting its banishment from its home”).
Shams al-Din Aflaki, Manaqib al-Arifin (14th century): stories of the first meeting, including Shams and Rumi’s books in the water (later hagiography; versions differ).

Rumi’s life: born 1207; settled in Konya; met Shams in Konya in 1244; Shams left in 1246, returned, then disappeared about 1247; the students’ jealousy is reported in Sultan Walad’s Ibtida-nama and Aflaki.
The “field beyond right and wrong”: a popular modern English version of a quatrain in the Divan-e Shams; paraphrased only, not quoted.
check: The books-in-the-water tale is labeled “one popular telling”; in some versions the books are thrown into a pool or fountain, in others into fire. The exchange (“What is this?” “Something you don’t know yet”) follows the common retelling loosely. Confirm.
Shams’s age (about sixty) and Rumi’s (about thirty-seven) in 1244. Confirm.
Teach: “the reed is the soul, cut from its source, which is god” is the usual Sufi reading. Confirm the wording.
